records.our_prose: The Southeast and Gulf run two bean seasons split by summer heat. Sow in spring after frost, then again in mid summer for a fall crop. The gap is real: through the hottest weeks blossoms drop and pods fail to set, so there is no point sowing into peak heat. Middle Georgia anchors the spring sowing to roughly mid March and the fall sowing to early July; the deeper South shifts spring earlier and fall later. Each sowing reaches a pickable crop in about 50 to 60 days.

records.our_prose: St. George's low-elevation Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) runs bush beans on one spring cycle only, per USU Extension's Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah. Direct-sow around March 15, the Group C (Tender) date for St. George, about two weeks ahead of the March 30 average last frost; the table's explicit local date runs earlier than a generic frost-relative rule would. Harvest begins about 55 days later, around May 9, and continues into late June. Once St. George's daytime highs push past 95°F and the county's own frost-and-elevation data show summer highs routinely reaching 100°F in June through August, blossoms drop and pods fail to set. USU documents fall planting for cool-season crops in the St. George area but gives no fall or summer-replant window for bush beans, so there is no second cycle here; frost returns around November 1, well after the plants have already stopped producing for the year.
